pages.subtitle: The quiet carpenter God chose to care for Jesus and Mary.
pages.intro: Joseph was a carpenter who lived in the town of Nazareth about 2,000 years ago. God chose him for a very special job: to be the husband of Mary and to care for Jesus as a father on earth. Joseph listened when God spoke to him, and he kept his family safe. Today he is the patron saint of the whole Church.
story_paragraphs: Almost everything we know about Joseph comes from the Bible, from the Gospels of Matthew and Luke. Joseph came from the family of the great King David. He lived and worked in the town of Nazareth as a carpenter.

Joseph was going to marry a young woman named Mary. Then he learned that Mary was going to have a baby. Joseph was a good and fair man, and he did not know what to do. In a dream, an angel told him not to be afraid. The child was from the Holy Spirit. So Joseph took Mary as his wife.
Jesus was born in the town of Bethlehem. Wise men called the Magi came to honor him there.
Soon there was danger. A king named Herod wanted to harm the child. An angel warned Joseph, and he took Mary and Jesus far away to the land of Egypt, where they would be safe.
After King Herod died, an angel told Joseph it was time to go home. Joseph brought his family back and settled in Nazareth. There he taught Jesus his own work, carpentry.

When Jesus was 12 years old, the family went to the Temple in Jerusalem. On the way home, Mary and Joseph could not find Jesus. They searched and searched. At last they found him in the Temple. That is the last time the Bible tells us about Joseph.

Joseph probably died before Jesus began teaching and healing. An old tradition says that Jesus and Mary were beside him when he died. That is why people ask Saint Joseph to pray for those who are dying.
Christians have honored Joseph more and more over the centuries. In 1870, Pope Pius IX named him the patron saint of the whole Church.

pages.subtitle: A young noblewoman who gave up riches to follow Jesus, as her friend Francis did.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Starting the Poor Clares and living simply for God

pages.intro: Clare grew up in a rich and important family in Assisi, Italy. When she was 18, she left it all behind to follow Jesus in the simple way that Saint Francis taught. Other women joined her. They became known as the Poor Clares. For more than 40 years, Clare lived at a little church called San Damiano, praying and caring for her sisters.
story_paragraphs: Clare was born in Assisi, Italy, in 1193 or 1194. Her family was rich and noble, which means they were among the most important people in town.
In Assisi, a young man named Francis had given up everything to live like Jesus. Clare wanted to follow Jesus in the same way.

On the evening of Palm Sunday, when Clare was 18, she left her family's home with a friend named Bona. They went to a little church called the Portiuncula, where Francis and his brothers were waiting. There, Francis cut off Clare's long hair, and she put on a rough, plain dress. It was a sign that she now belonged to God alone.

Soon Clare and her first companions settled beside the small church of San Damiano. They owned nothing and spent their days in prayer and work. More women came to join them. Their community became known as the Poor Clares.

Clare asked the Pope for something unusual. She did not ask for money or land. She asked for the right to own nothing at all, so that she and her sisters would depend only on God. This was called the "Privilege of Poverty."

Clare was the leader of the sisters, but she served them. She took care of the sisters who were sick. She was also the first woman in the history of the Church to write a rule of life and send it to the Pope for his approval.
Twice, soldiers came to attack the convent. Each time, Clare held up the Blessed Sacrament and prayed, and the soldiers went away.
Clare lived at San Damiano for more than 40 years. She died on August 11, 1253. Just two years later, in 1255, Pope Alexander IV declared her a saint.

pages.subtitle: A Franciscan friar whose preaching helped many people come back to God.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: His preaching and teaching, and prayers for lost things

pages.intro: Anthony was born in Portugal about 800 years ago. He wanted to be a missionary in a faraway land, but sickness and a storm changed his plans. He landed in Italy instead. There, people discovered that he was a wonderful preacher. Crowds came to hear him explain the Gospel. Today many people ask Saint Anthony to pray when something is lost.
story_paragraphs: Anthony was born around 1195 in Lisbon, the capital city of Portugal. His family was wealthy. His parents named him Fernando.
When Fernando was a teenager, he joined a group of priests who lived and prayed together. He studied the Bible for many years.

In 1220, something changed his life. The bodies of five Franciscan friars were brought to his city. They had been killed in Morocco for preaching about Jesus. Fernando was so moved by their courage that he became a Franciscan too. He took a new name, Anthony.

Anthony set out for Morocco to be a missionary. But he became very sick and had to turn back. Then a storm blew his ship off course. Instead of reaching Portugal, he landed on the island of Sicily, in Italy.

In 1221, Anthony went to a great meeting of the Franciscans in Assisi. There he met Saint Francis. Afterward, Anthony went to live quietly in a small friary. Hardly anyone knew how much he had learned.

One day, Anthony was asked to preach at a special Mass. Everyone was amazed. He spoke so clearly and knew the Bible so well that his leaders sent him out to preach. Saint Francis himself wrote to him, "I would like you to teach the brethren theology." Theology is the study of God.
Anthony preached in Italy and France. Many people who had left the Church came back after hearing him. He also taught other friars, and he spoke up for the poor.

Anthony died on June 13, 1231, near the city of Padua, Italy. He was only about 36 years old. Pope Gregory IX declared him a saint the very next year. In 1946, Pope Pius XII named him a Doctor of the Church.

pages.subtitle: A priest who loved Mary and gave his life to save another man.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Giving his life in place of another prisoner

pages.intro: Maximilian Kolbe was a Franciscan priest from Poland who loved Mary, the Mother of Jesus. He started magazines and built a huge friary to tell people about her. During a terrible war, he was sent to a prison camp. When a guard chose a husband and father to die, Father Kolbe stepped forward and offered to take the man's place.
story_paragraphs: Maximilian Kolbe was born on January 8, 1894, in the town of Zduńska Wola, in Poland. His parents named him Raymond, and they taught him to love Mary, the Mother of Jesus.

When Raymond was 12, he said that Mary came to him. He later explained, "I asked the Mother of God what was to become of me. Then she came to me holding two crowns: one white, the other red." The white crown stood for a pure heart. The red crown stood for giving his life for Jesus. Raymond said he would accept them both.
Soon afterward, Raymond and his older brother joined the Franciscans. He was given a new name, Maximilian. He studied in Rome and became a priest in 1918.

Father Kolbe wanted the whole world to know and love Mary. In 1917, he had started a group to spread devotion to her. He began a magazine. Then, in 1927, he built a new friary near the city of Warsaw. He called it Niepokalanów, which means "City of the Immaculate." About 700 friars and workers came to live and work there.
In 1930, Father Kolbe and four other friars traveled all the way to Japan. They started a friary in the city of Nagasaki. After a few years, poor health sent him back to Poland.

In 1939, a great war began, and the army of Nazi Germany took over Poland. Father Kolbe helped people who had to flee their homes, including Jewish families. In February 1941, he was arrested and sent to a prison camp called Auschwitz.

That summer, a prisoner escaped. To punish everyone, the guards picked ten men to die. One of them, Franciszek Gajowniczek, had a wife and young children. Father Kolbe offered to take his place, and the guards agreed.
Father Kolbe was killed on August 14, 1941. Franciszek lived through the war. In 1982, he was there when Pope John Paul II declared Maximilian Kolbe a saint.

pages.subtitle: Stolen from her home as a child, she found freedom, faith, and a heart full of forgiveness.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Her forgiveness and her joyful trust in God

pages.intro: Josephine Bakhita was born in Sudan, a country in Africa. When she was a little girl, she was kidnapped and sold as a slave. After many years of suffering, she was taken to Italy. There she learned about God, became free, and was baptized. She became a religious sister, loved by everyone for her gentle smile. She forgave the people who had hurt her.
story_paragraphs: Bakhita was born around 1869 in a village in Darfur, a part of Sudan, in Africa.
When she was about nine years old, men who sold people as slaves kidnapped her. She was so frightened that she forgot her own name. The kidnappers called her Bakhita, which means "fortunate."

For years, Bakhita was sold from one owner to another in the slave markets of two cities, El Obeid and Khartoum. She was treated very cruelly. Slavery is a great wrong, and no person should ever be owned by another.

At last, in Khartoum, an Italian official named Callisto Legnani bought her. For the first time since she was taken, someone treated her kindly. When he went home to Italy in 1884, Bakhita went too. In Italy, she lived with a family called the Michielis and took care of their little daughter.

In 1888, Bakhita and the little girl stayed for some months with the Canossian Sisters in the city of Venice. There Bakhita learned about God. She had wondered about him for a long time. She said, "Seeing the sun, the moon and the stars, I said to myself: Who could be the Master of these beautiful things?"

When the family came to take her back, Bakhita chose to stay with the sisters. Under the law of Italy, she was free to decide. On January 9, 1890, she was baptized and given the name Josephine. She said with joy, "Here, I became a daughter of God!"
On December 8, 1896, Josephine became a Canossian Sister. She lived for about 50 years in the town of Schio. She cooked, sewed, and answered the door. People loved her gentle smile and her goodness.
Josephine forgave the men who had kidnapped and hurt her. She died on February 8, 1947. Pope John Paul II declared her a saint on October 1, 2000.

pages.subtitle: A rich American who gave away her fortune, and her whole life, to build schools for children others had left out.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Building schools for Native American and African American children

pages.intro: Katharine Drexel grew up in one of the richest families in America. She saw that many Native American and African American children had no good schools. She asked the Pope to send missionaries to help them. He asked her to become one herself. So Katharine became a religious sister and spent her fortune, and her whole life, building schools and missions across the country.
story_paragraphs: Katharine Drexel was born on November 26, 1858, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Her father, Francis, was a very rich banker. Her mother died soon after Katharine was born, and her father later married a kind woman named Emma.

Katharine's parents taught their daughters that their money was only "loaned to them" by God and was meant to be shared. Twice a week, the family opened their home and gave food, clothing, and rent money to people in need.
In 1884, Katharine traveled to the western part of the United States with her father. She saw Native American families living in great poverty. She never forgot it.

The next year, her father died. He left a huge fortune to Katharine and her two sisters. The sisters began giving money to missions and schools. In January 1887, Katharine visited Pope Leo XIII in Rome. She asked him to send more missionaries to help Native Americans. The Pope answered, "But why not be a missionary yourself, my child?"

Katharine thought and prayed. In 1889, she entered a convent to learn how to be a sister. On February 12, 1891, she made her vows and began a new religious family, the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament. They would serve Native American and African American people.

At that time, many people treated Black and Native American families unfairly, and some were angry at Mother Katharine for helping them. Once, someone smashed every window in one of her new schools. She kept going.
Mother Katharine and her sisters started nearly 60 schools and missions. In 1925, she founded Xavier University in New Orleans, a Catholic university for African American students.

In 1935, Mother Katharine had a serious heart attack. She spent her last years quietly in prayer. She died on March 3, 1955, at the age of 96. Pope John Paul II declared her a saint on October 1, 2000.

pages.subtitle: A humble brother in Peru who cared for the sick, the poor, and even stray animals.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Caring for sick and poor people of every background

pages.intro: Martin de Porres was born in Lima, Peru, more than 400 years ago. His mother was a free Black woman, and his father was a Spanish nobleman. Many people looked down on Martin because of who his parents were. He answered with kindness. As a Dominican brother, he cared for the sick, fed the hungry, started a school for poor children, and was gentle with animals.
story_paragraphs: Martin de Porres was born on December 9, 1579, in Lima, the capital city of Peru, in South America. His father, Juan de Porres, was a Spanish nobleman. His mother was a free Black woman who had once been a slave. Martin had a sister.
Martin's father left the family, and Martin grew up poor. In those days, many people treated a child like Martin unfairly because his parents came from different races.
As a boy, Martin went to work for a barber. Long ago, barbers did more than cut hair. They also cared for sick people. Martin learned how to treat wounds and give medicine.

When Martin was 15, he went to live at a Dominican friary in Lima. At first he was only a helper, doing the humblest jobs, such as cleaning. It was not the custom then to accept a man of mixed race as a brother. But the friars saw Martin's goodness, and in time they welcomed him as a full brother.

Brother Martin took care of the sick friars in the infirmary, a room for people who are ill. He also worked in the kitchen and the laundry. He gave food and money to people in need. He cared for Africans who had just been brought to Peru as slaves, and for Native people. He raised money so that poor young women could marry.
Martin also started a school in Lima for children who were orphans or had been abandoned. It was one of the first schools for poor children in the Americas.
Martin was kind to animals, too. He cared for stray cats and dogs. Once he nursed a badly hurt dog until it was well. He was even gentle with the mice in the kitchen.
Martin died on the evening of November 3, 1639. The whole city honored him. Pope John XXIII declared him a saint on May 6, 1962.

pages.subtitle: A priest who became a father, teacher, and friend to boys who had no one.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Teaching and caring for young people

pages.intro: John Bosco was born on a small farm in Italy. When he was nine, he had a dream that showed him his life's work: helping young people. He became a priest in the city of Turin. There he gave poor boys a place to play, learn, pray, and train for a job. People called him Don Bosco. Today the Salesians carry on his work all over the world.
story_paragraphs: John Bosco was born on August 16, 1815, at a place called Becchi, in northern Italy. His father died before John was two years old. His mother, Margaret, raised him and taught him to love God.

When John was nine, he had a dream he never forgot. It showed him that God wanted him to spend his life helping young people. Even as a boy, John gathered other children for games, and he mixed in prayers and lessons about God.
John became a priest in June 1841, in the city of Turin. People called him Don Bosco. "Don" is a title for a priest in Italy.

In Turin, Don Bosco met many boys who were poor and alone. They had no school, no work, and no one to guide them. He began gathering them on Sundays to play, learn, and pray. He called this gathering the Oratory.

In the spring of 1846, the Oratory found a home in a part of Turin called Valdocco. Don Bosco added a place for boys to live, and classrooms. Then he opened workshops where boys could learn a trade: tailoring, bookbinding, carpentry, printing, and metalwork.

Don Bosco had his own way of teaching. He did not believe in harsh punishments. He guided young people with reason, with faith, and with loving kindness. He told them, "It is enough that you are young for me to love you very much."

On December 18, 1859, Don Bosco and eighteen young men began a new religious family to carry on this work. They are called the Salesians, after Saint Francis de Sales. In 1872, with Saint Mary Mazzarello, he began a family of sisters to help girls. In 1875, he sent the first Salesian missionaries to Argentina.
Don Bosco died on January 31, 1888. He was declared a saint on April 1, 1934.

pages.subtitle: Known as Padre Pio, a humble friar who spent his life praying and helping people come back to God.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Prayer, hearing confessions, and care for the sick

pages.intro: Padre Pio was a Capuchin friar and priest who lived in a small town in Italy. "Padre" means "Father." He spent many hours each day praying and hearing confessions. People came from far away to ask for his help. He also built a hospital for the sick. He said of himself, "I only want to be a poor friar who prays."
story_paragraphs: Padre Pio was born on May 25, 1887, in Pietrelcina, a small town in southern Italy. His parents, Grazio and Maria Giuseppa Forgione, named him Francesco.

When Francesco was 15, he joined the Capuchins, a branch of the Franciscan family. He was given a new name, Brother Pio. On August 10, 1910, he was ordained a priest. From then on, people called him Padre Pio.

Padre Pio was often sick, and for several years he had to live at home with his family. In September 1916, he was sent to a friary in a mountain town called San Giovanni Rotondo. He stayed there for the rest of his life.
On September 20, 1918, wounds like the wounds of Jesus on the cross appeared on Padre Pio's body. They are called the stigmata. They stayed for 50 years, and they caused him pain.

News of the wounds spread. Crowds began to come. Leaders of the Church wanted to be careful, so they studied Padre Pio closely. For some years, they did not allow him to say Mass in public or to hear confessions. This was very hard for him, but he obeyed humbly and did not complain. Later, the limits were lifted.

For more than fifty years, Padre Pio welcomed the people who came to him. He heard confessions from morning until night, helping people tell God they were sorry and begin again. He spent much of the day, and a large part of the night, in prayer. He said, "In books we seek God, in prayer we find him. Prayer is the key which opens God's heart."
Padre Pio also cared about people who were sick. With gifts from many helpers, he built a hospital. It opened on May 5, 1956. Its name means "Home for the Relief of Suffering."
Padre Pio died on September 23, 1968, at age 81. Pope John Paul II declared him a saint on June 16, 2002.

pages.subtitle: A humble sister from Poland who told the world about the mercy of Jesus.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Sharing the message of Divine Mercy

pages.intro: Faustina Kowalska grew up on a poor farm in Poland and went to school for only three years. She became a religious sister and worked as a cook, a gardener, and a doorkeeper. She wrote in her diary that Jesus asked her to tell the whole world about his mercy. Her message can be said in five words: "Jesus, I trust in You."
story_paragraphs: Faustina was born on August 25, 1905, in the village of Głogowiec, in Poland. Her parents named her Helena. She was the third of ten children, and her family were poor farmers.

When Helena was seven years old, she first felt that God was calling her to belong to him in a special way. She went to school for only three years. At 16, she left home to work as a housekeeper so she could help her parents.

Helena wanted to become a religious sister, but at first her parents said no. Then, she said, she saw Jesus suffering, and she knew she must not wait any longer. In August 1925, she entered the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy. She was given a new name, Sister Mary Faustina.

For thirteen years, Sister Faustina lived in several convents in Poland and nearby. Her jobs were simple. She was a cook, a gardener, and a doorkeeper. Few people knew what was happening in her prayer.

Sister Faustina wrote in her diary that on February 22, 1931, she saw Jesus. Two rays of light came from his heart, one red and one pale. She wrote that he told her, "Paint an image according to the model you see, with these words written: Jesus, I trust in You."

Mercy means God's love that forgives. Sister Faustina wrote that Jesus wanted everyone to know that his mercy is greater than any sin, and that people should trust him and be merciful to one another. She also wrote down a prayer called the Chaplet of Divine Mercy.
The priests who guided Sister Faustina asked her to write everything in a diary. Today that diary is read in many languages.
Sister Faustina became sick with tuberculosis, a serious illness of the lungs. She died in Kraków on October 5, 1938, when she was only 33. Pope John Paul II declared her a saint on April 30, 2000.

canonical.match_title: St. Damien de Veuster of Moloka’i

pages.subtitle: A priest who went to live with sick people everyone else was afraid of, and became one of them.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Caring for people with leprosy on the island of Molokai

pages.intro: Father Damien was a priest from Belgium who became a missionary in Hawaii. In those days, people who had a disease called leprosy were sent away to live on a lonely piece of land on the island of Molokai. Father Damien asked to go and live with them. He stayed for 16 years, caring for them like a father, until he died of the same disease.
story_paragraphs: Damien was born on January 3, 1840, in the village of Tremelo, in Belgium. His parents named him Jozef, and his family called him Jef. He was one of seven children.

In 1859, Jozef joined a religious family called the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts. He took the name Damien. His brother belonged to the same religious family and was chosen to be a missionary in Hawaii. But his brother became sick, and Damien asked to go in his place.
Damien arrived in Honolulu, Hawaii, on March 19, 1864. Two months later, he was ordained a priest.

At that time, there was no cure for a disease called leprosy. People were very afraid of catching it. The government of Hawaii sent everyone who had it to live at Kalaupapa, a piece of land on the island of Molokai, with the sea on three sides and tall cliffs behind. They had to leave their families, and most never saw them again.

In 1873, Father Damien asked his bishop for permission to go and live there. On May 10, 1873, he set out. More than 800 people were living at Kalaupapa. The bishop told them that Father Damien would be a father to them.

There was a great deal to do. Father Damien built and repaired houses with his own hands. He helped the people plant crops and start schools. He cared for the sick with his own hands. When someone died, he built the coffin and dug the grave himself.

In December 1884, Father Damien learned that he had caught leprosy too. He kept working as long as he could. In his last years, others came to help, including Mother Marianne Cope and her sisters and a man named Joseph Dutton.
Father Damien died on April 15, 1889. He was 49 years old. He was declared a saint on October 11, 2009.

pages.subtitle: A humble doorkeeper in Canada who welcomed thousands and led them to Saint Joseph.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Praying with the sick and his love for Saint Joseph

pages.intro: Brother André was a small, sickly man from Canada who could barely read. His job was to answer the door at a school in Montreal. He did it for about 40 years. Sick and worried people came to see him, and he prayed with them to Saint Joseph. When Brother André died, more than a million people came to say goodbye.
story_paragraphs: André was born on August 9, 1845, in a village near Montreal, in Canada. His parents named him Alfred. He was so weak as a baby that he was baptized the very next day. He was the ninth of thirteen children.

Alfred's father cut wood and built things for a living. When Alfred was nine, his father was killed when a tree fell on him. Two years later, his mother died of an illness. At 12 years old, Alfred was an orphan. An aunt and uncle took him in.

Alfred was often sick, and he had almost no schooling. He tried many jobs: farm worker, baker's helper, shoemaker. When he was 18, he went to the United States and worked in cotton mills for about four years.

Back in Canada, a priest saw how deeply Alfred prayed. He encouraged him to join the Congregation of Holy Cross, a religious family of priests and brothers. Alfred arrived in 1870, when he was 25. He took the name Brother André.
The brothers almost sent him away because his health was so poor. But the bishop of Montreal spoke up for him, and he was allowed to stay.

Brother André was given the job of doorkeeper at a boys' school. He also cleaned, ran errands, cut the students' hair, and cared for them when they were sick. He liked to joke, "My superiors showed me the door, and there I stayed for forty years."

People who were sick or sad began coming to the door to ask for his prayers. Brother André loved Saint Joseph. He prayed with the visitors and gave them medals of Saint Joseph. Many said they were healed. Brother André always said that he did not heal anyone. It was Saint Joseph who prayed for them.

In 1904, Brother André built a small chapel to honor Saint Joseph on the hill across from the school. Over the years, it grew into a great church. Brother André died on January 6, 1937. Pope Benedict XVI declared him a saint on October 17, 2010.

choices.text: A small chapel to honor Saint Joseph

quiz.explanation: His small chapel opened on October 16, 1904. Over the years, it grew into a great church.
